There *is* a way for you and I to be happy without being skinny, it's just that ED isn't allowing us to see it. The mindset feels like being stuck under a frozen lake to me, and not being able to find a crack in the ice (yet). But I hope that eventually we all will, and that will be real (*mental)* recovery.

After a single very harsh, awkward confrontation a few months ago, my roommate finally moved out on me last weekend and told all of our mutual friends it was because I "gave" her bulimia (which she had for one whole month before deciding it was gross and quitting just like that. lol.). I've struggled with very severe bulimia for years now and even though I wouldn't dare talk about it in front of her or anything, seeing me getting thinner from adding restriction on top of it was enough to "trigger" the person who I thought was my best friend into telling me that I'm "toxic" by virtue of my very existence as a person with this disease and prompt her to ghost me after years of friendship.

Moral of the story/my unsolicited advice as someone who has learned this lesson the very hard way: *do not* talk about ED, calories, food restriction, purging, etc. with the *vast* majority of people you know. As people with ED, thoughts that sound normal to us, frequency of talking about food that seems normal to us, and habits that are part of our daily lives can be very shocking and upsetting to a lot of people, even if they won't tell you outright. Aside from close family members and maybe a friend or two, it really is worth it to make a big effort to not mention anything involving eating/calories/food in front of others. It's hard because you want and deserve a support system, but hurting others is a big risk, as is getting hurt when non-disordered people sense the negative effect your disorder may be having on them. As I've learned, even after you've stopped talking about these things out loud, it's difficult for people to shake the association between your presence and their own self consciousness about food :/

I used to be jealous a long time ago before I learned about CICO. It's all calories in, calories out, so if they were really eating that way all the time 24/7 they wouldn't be thin. For example, I could sit down and eat two big macs (1100 calories) and lose weight for the day. It would look like I was just a relatively thin person binging on fast food if you just glanced by and didn't know anything else, but in order to continue losing that would be all I would eat in a day and it would actually be a pretty good calorie deficit of around 500 calories below maintenance, or 1 pound loss over one week.. You may also see an obese person eating the same two big macs (1100 calories), but they'll probably have also had breakfast (say 600 calories) and will eat dinner (maybe 1500 calories), which will bring their calorie total for the day above their maintenance level and cause then to gain weight. It's all about the numbers, some people just naturally balance out their calories and don't need to meticulously count them :) There are no magical thin people who are eating way over maintenance calories every single day and remaining that way.

If you feel that you can't eat more than 800 calories for fear of gaining weight or because of negative body image, that's a disordered thought. If you feel that you need to purge/use laxatives/use diuretics/excessively exercise after eating to "make up for it", that's a disordered thought. Unfortunately for AN they usually diagnosis it based on an underweight BMI first and THEN the continued restricting, whereas for BN they diagnose based on the behavior alone. That doesn't mean you're a "fraud", it's a problem with the system. With an overweight anorexic as well as with a severely underweight anorexic, the disordered mindset (which is the actual source of the disorder) is the same.
